standard.title: Develop civic inquiry questions
standard.description: develop questions to investigate Australia's political and legal systems, and contemporary civic issues
standard.prior_knowledge: Students have developed questions about civic topics at Year 7 level (AC9HC7S01) in the context of Australia's political and legal systems at introductory scope. The gap this descriptor fills is development of questioning at a more sophisticated level — including the distinction between key questions and related sub-questions, and the move from narrower factual questions to open-ended questions that drive investigation of contemporary civic issues.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students develop questions — including key questions and related sub-questions — to investigate Australia's political and legal systems and contemporary civic issues, demonstrating capacity to generate both closed and open-ended questions and to identify current events as inquiry starting points.

nodes.label: Closed and open-ended civic questions
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can distinguish between closed (factual, single-answer) and open-ended (investigative, multiple-perspective) questions in the context of civic topics, and generate examples of each.
nodes.minimum_width: Write one closed and one open-ended question about the same civic topic, and explain the difference in what each question can investigate.
nodes.typical_width: Develop a range of closed and open-ended questions about a civic topic — for example, 'What are the main features of a democracy?', 'How are laws made?' and 'What is the relationship between democracy and active citizenship?' — and explain the different investigative purposes of each question type.
wider: Analyse a set of provided questions about a civic issue, categorising them as closed or open-ended and explaining which would generate richer investigation and why

Investigate how different question types serve different purposes in civic inquiry — when factual closed questions are necessary versus when open-ended questions are needed to explore perspectives and contestation
Practise rewriting closed civic questions as open-ended ones, examining what changes about what the question can investigate
nodes.hinge_reason: The closed/open-ended distinction is the foundation for developing inquiry questions that actually drive investigation. If students cannot distinguish between them, their key questions will tend to be factual closed questions that limit investigation to information retrieval rather than perspective analysis.

response_modes.reason: Students often default to factual questions because they feel safer. Invest in the reasoning scaffold: what kind of thinking does each question type demand, and when does civic inquiry require open-ended questions?

success_criteria: Can write a closed question and an open-ended question about the same civic topic
Can explain the difference in investigative purpose between the two question types

nodes.label: Key question and related sub-questions
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can develop a key inquiry question and a set of related sub-questions to investigate a civic issue, demonstrating that the sub-questions scaffold investigation toward the key question.
nodes.minimum_width: Develop a key inquiry question about a civic issue and at least two related sub-questions that help investigate it.
nodes.typical_width: Develop a key question and related sub-questions to investigate a civic issue — for example, 'How do young people effectively participate in democratic processes to influence issues that impact on them?' or 'How did public opinion help in persuading the government on the importance of providing a National Disability Insurance Scheme?' — ensuring the sub-questions build cumulatively toward the key question.
wider: Develop a question framework for investigating a current civic issue, evaluating whether the sub-questions together cover the factual, perspective and evaluative dimensions needed to fully address the key question
Critique a provided set of inquiry questions for a civic issue — identifying gaps, overlaps or sub-questions that don't scaffold toward the key question
Revise an initial question framework after a first round of research, adding sub-questions that address gaps uncovered during investigation
nodes.hinge_reason: The ability to structure a key question supported by related sub-questions is the organisational framework for all subsequent inquiry work in S02–S05. If students cannot generate a coherent question structure, their research, analysis and argument tasks lack direction and focus.

response_modes.reason: The relationship between a key question and sub-questions is a scaffolding relationship — sub-questions should cumulatively build the investigation needed to address the key question. This requires explicit reasoning about inquiry design, not just question writing.

success_criteria: Can develop a key inquiry question about a civic issue
Can write at least two sub-questions that clearly scaffold toward the key question rather than restating it or going off on tangents

nodes.label: Current events as inquiry starting points
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify current events and issues as starting points for civic inquiry questions, connecting contemporary events to the political and legal systems they are studying.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify one current event and explain how it could generate civic inquiry questions, writing at least one example question.
nodes.typical_width: Consider current events to generate ideas for research — for example, how Australian governments have developed media campaigns on public health issues, or why media coverage of the National Agreement on Closing the Gap reflects changing perspectives on Australia's national identity — and develop inquiry questions that connect current events to the political and legal concepts being studied.
wider: Monitor a current civic issue over a period of time and develop evolving inquiry questions as new information comes to light — practising adaptive inquiry

Examine how different current events raise different kinds of civic questions (legal questions, political participation questions, identity questions) and practise matching question types to issue types
Investigate how the same current event can generate different inquiry questions depending on the civic focus: political participation, law, identity or citizenship

response_modes.reason: Connecting inquiry to current events requires exposure to a range of events and issue types. Widening across different types of civic events — legal, political, identity-related — builds the skill of recognising inquiry-worthy issues.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Current events as inquiry starting points builds authentic civic engagement. Width across different types of civic events — political, legal, identity — develops the skill of recognising which framework to apply to which situation, which is a core transferable capability.
success_criteria: Can identify a current event that connects to a civic concept studied in Year 8
Can develop at least one inquiry question that links the event to political, legal or civic content
